title: Half is enough (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:13)
hookLine: no one leaves the world with even half their desires fulfilled
tomorrow: Abraham and Moses pleaded and weren't answered. who was?

lines: ONE IN THE MORNING. FIVE THINGS.
cards: One in the morning. The cart has five things in it, and the plan was one. The app offers a sixth, a slightly better version of the third.
A bar at the top says free shipping is only a few dollars away. The thumb hovers, then taps. The screen says thank you.
And before the box has even left the warehouse, a new tab is open, looking at the next thing. Nobody in this scene is a villain. This is just what wanting does.
A midrash on Ecclesiastes saw this exact loop, long before anyone had a cart.

teach.b: Ecclesiastes says it plainly: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver." The midrash, Ecclesiastes Rabbah, turns that line into arithmetic.
No one, it says, leaves the world with even half of what they wanted in hand.
Have a hundred, and you want two hundred. Reach two hundred, and you want four hundred. Watch what the math does.

Every gain doubles the finish line, so the half you were chasing slides further off each time. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: by the midrash's math, the more you get, the further you are from half.
So the sages don't promise that one day you'll finally have it all. They point the other way.

If half can't be reached by adding, then enough has to come from somewhere else: from choosing. Elsewhere, in Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma asks, who is rich? His answer: the one who is happy with their portion.
Not the one with the most. The one who stepped out of the doubling. This isn't a vow to own nothing.
Jewish blessings are said over bread, over wine, over new clothes. It's one small exit from the loop: name a want, and let it go unfed.
Half is enough, because the whole was never coming.

how: Jewish teaching on contentment often turns to Ben Zoma in Pirkei Avot 4:1: who is rich? the one who rejoices in their portion. Blessings over food and new things are one daily way the tradition practices enough.

o: enough is chosen, because wanting doubles with every gain
a rule to give half of what you own to the poor
a saying that half a loaf beats having no bread

games.q: the arithmetic of wanting — tap the pairs.
p: silver doesn't satisfy the one who loves it
rich is happy with your portion
no one leaves with it in hand

s: the midrash says wanting things is wrong
it says wanting never finishes. enough comes from choosing, not from owning nothing.
by the midrash's math, more makes half further away
a hundred wants two hundred, two hundred wants four: every gain doubles the finish line.
Ben Zoma says the rich are the ones with the most
he says rich is the one who is happy with their portion.

games.q: your cousin just got a raise and is already pricing a bigger apartment, a newer car and a second phone. by the midrash, what's the honest question to ask her?
o: how much would be enough, since the finish line keeps doubling?
can you afford it, since debt is the only real danger here?
why want anything at all, since wanting is the real problem?
games.why: Ecclesiastes Rabbah doesn't condemn wanting; it shows the finish line doubling with every gain. enough has to be chosen.

practice: Open the place your wants collect: a cart, a wishlist, a row of tabs, a note of things to buy. Choose one item and remove it, just for today, and look at what's left once that one stops doubling.
If nothing is saved anywhere, name one want quietly to yourself and let it sit there, unfed, while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Half is enough: the midrash's arithmetic of wanting. Have a hundred, want two hundred; nobody reaches half by adding.

orig.note: Hebrew: half. the midrash says no one leaves the world with half their desire in hand.

carryVoice: Your line: half is enough. The whole was never coming anyway. Thirty days into reading midrash.
